IPT.evidence_source: [page/1/Text/3] To address these limitations in the literature, we developed a 10-session combined cognitive–behavioral and family education intervention for children. The intervention included three distinct features. First, the intervention included a family education session designed to promote generalization of skills to key environmental contexts (home, school, community), encourage parents to support the learning that was achieved through the group sessions, and foster positive attitudes towards the skills emphasized in the intervention. Second, consistent with Meichenbaum and Biemiller's emphasis on the importance of increasing levels of self-direction in moving from skill acquisition to mastery in CBT interventions (Meichenbaum & Biemiller; 1998), the intervention was designed to address the progression from skill acquisition, to skill consolidation (through practice), to assuming a consulting or teaching role. Intervention sessions were structured around the development of a videotape by the children, which was shown to parents at "family night," and provided multiple opportunities for children to practice and consolidate the skills introduced in each CBT session. During family night each child then assumed the role of "consultant" as they taught their parents the skills emphasized in the group session. Finally, to address the high rate of comorbid symptoms/disorders and adjustment problems observed among youth with depression, the intervention included generic CBT components such as problem-solving and social skills training as well as depression-specific CBT components similar to those included in other cognitive–behavioral interventions for depression (Clarke et al., 1999; Lewinsohn, Clarke, Hops, & Andrews, 1990).

dxgive.evidence_source: [page/2/Text/2] Although initial development and testing was conducted with clinical samples of children meeting criteria for major depression or dysthymic disorder, a school-based sample with depressive symptoms was used for this phase of the intervention development to permit a relatively rapid examination of intervention acceptability, feasibility, and effects.
